questions.qtext:
To check for conflict serializability of any schedule, we draw its Precedence graph. In the precedence graph we have a node for each transaction $\text{T}_i$ and An edge from $\text{T}_i$ to $\text{T}_j$ whenever an action in $\text{T}_i$ conflicts with, and comes before an action in $\text{T}_j.$

For a conflict serializable schedule $\text{S},$ which of the following is guaranteed to give a serial schedule that is conflict equivalent to $\text{S},$ in the precedence Graph?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

B is correct because DFS and BFS will lead to an order even if there exists a cycle in the precedence graph but topological sorting is only possible in the cycle-free graph. The cycle in the precedence graph indicates non-conflict serializability. Also even if there is no cycle in the precedence graph, DFS, BFS need not give an equivalent serial order.

For example, take the following graph :

  • $\text{T}_1 \rightarrow \text{T}_2, \text{T}_3$
  • $\text{T}_3 \rightarrow \text{T}_2$

If we start at $\text{T}_1,$ then DFS, BFS may give $\text{T}_1, \text{T}_2, \text{T}_3,$ which is Not equivalent serial order.

Suppose that transaction $\mathrm{T} 1$ aborts after the following sequence of read write operations in the given schedule below : $$\text{Write1(X); Write2(X); Write1(Y)};\; \operatorname{Read3}(\mathrm{Y}) ;\; \operatorname{Read}4(\mathrm{X}) ;\; \operatorname{Read}4(\mathrm{Z})$$
Which of the other transactions would need to be rolled back?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 19)
A Recoverable execution is one which allows commits only when all transactions that wrote data items read by the committing transaction have committed.
An execution is recoverable if, for every transaction $\mathrm{T}$ that commits, $\text{T's}$ commit follows the commit of every transaction from which $\mathrm{T}$ read.
Since, $\text{T1}$ aborts, we see which transaction has read from $\text{T1},$ that is only $\text{T3}.$ So, $\text{T3}$ should abort as well.

questions.qtext: Consider a database schedule of two transactions $\text{T1, T2}.\;\text{T1}$ first reads $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ and then writes $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}.\; \text{T2}$ reads and writes $\text{A}$ then reads and writes $\text{B}.$ Consider the following statements. Which of the following statements are correct?

options.text: Every concurrent/interleaved execution of these transactions will lead to a conflict serializable schedule.
Every concurrent/interleaved execution of these transactions will lead to a view serializable schedule.
If a concurrent/interleaved execution of these transactions lead to a non-conflict serializable schedule then that schedule is also non-view serializable.
If a concurrent/interleaved execution of these transactions lead to a non-view serializable schedule then that schedule is also non-conflict serializable.

Source solution 2 (score: 12)
Given below is an example schedule that is not (conflict) serializable :
$$\mathrm{R} 1[\mathrm{~A}] \rightarrow \mathrm{R} 1[\mathrm{~B}] \rightarrow \mathrm{R} 2[\mathrm{~A}] \rightarrow \mathrm{W} 2[\mathrm{~A}] \rightarrow \mathrm{R} 2[\mathrm{~B}] \rightarrow \mathrm{W} 1[\mathrm{~A}] $$$$ \rightarrow \mathrm{W} 1[\mathrm{~B}] \rightarrow \mathrm{W} 2[\mathrm{~B}]\rightarrow \mathrm{C} 1 \rightarrow \mathrm{C} 2$$
A schedule is (conflict) serializable if it contains the same transactions and operations as a serial schedule and the order of all conflicting operations (read/writes to the same objects by different transactions) is also the same. In the above schedule, $\text{T1}$ reads $\text{A}$ before $\text{T2}$ writes $\mathrm{A}.$ However, $\text{T1}$ writes $\text{A}$ after $\text{T2}$ reads and writes it.

The schedule is thus clearly not serializable. Additionally, according to the above schedule, the final content of object $\mathrm{A}$ is written by $\mathrm{T} 1$ and the final content of object $\text{B}$ is written by $\text{T2}.$ Such a result is not possible in any serial execution, where transactions execute one after the other in sequence. Not view serializable implies not conflict serializable.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following schedule $\text{S :}$
$$\text{start1; start2; r1(A); r2(B); w2(A); w1(B);}$$
$\text{“start #"}$ means beginning of transaction $\#,$ then which of the following is/are Incorrect?

options.text: $\mathrm{S}$ is possible under basic Timestamp Ordering (T/O) protocol.
$\mathrm{S}$ is possible under THOMAS WRITE RULE Timestamp Ordering (T/O) protocol.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 18)

In the precedence graph \(G\) corresponding to the schedule \(S\) (where we denote transaction \(\#1\) as \(T_1\), and transaction \(\#2\) as \(T_2\)), we have both the edges \(T_1 \rightarrow T_2\) (as \(r_1(A)\) conflicts with \(w_2(A)\)), and \(T_2 \rightarrow T_1\) (as \(r_2(B)\) conflicts with \(w_1(B)\)). Thus, there is cycle in the graph \(G\), and so, the schedule \(S\) is not conflict-serializable. So, option the \((C)\) is false.

In the schedule \(S\), \(r_1(A)\) and \(r_2(B)\) read in the original values of the data items \(A\) and \(B\), respectively, in the database, whereas, in any serial schedule, at least one of those reads read in the modified value of the concerned data item, thus causing a violation of the first requirement for view serializability. Therefore, the schedule \(S\) is not view-serializable. So, option the \((D)\) is false.

The basic timestamp ordering protocol produces conflict-serializable schedules, whereas the timestamp ordering protocol with Thomas write rule produces conflict-serializable schedules along with a few view-serializable schedules. If a schedule itself isn’t view-serializable, then none of these variants of the timestamp ordering protocol helps. So, both the options \((A)\) and \((B)\) are false.

Correct Answer : \((A), (B), (C), (D)\)

Source solution 2 (score: 9)

Answer: A,B,C,D.

Each transaction $\mathrm{Ti}$ is issued a timestamp $\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Ti}$ ) when it enters the system.
If an old transaction $\mathrm{Ti}$ has timestamp $\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Ti})$, a new transaction $\mathrm{Tj}$ has timestamp $\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Tj})$ where $\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Ti})<\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Tj})$.

So, Assume $\text{TS(T1) = 1, TS(T2) = 2}$

When $\text{T1}$ performs $\mathrm{W}(\mathrm{B}), \mathrm{RTS}(\mathrm{B})=2$, So, $\mathrm{W_1}(\mathrm{B})$ is rejected by basic $\mathrm{T} / \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{T} 1$ is rollback. Thomas write rule also doesn’t allow this schedule.

Thomas write rule : When $\text{Ti}$ attempts to write data item $\text{Q},$ if $\mathrm{TS}(\mathrm{Ti})<\mathrm{W}-$timestamp $(\mathrm{Q})$, then $\text{Ti}$ is attempting to write an obsolete value of $\text{{Q}}$. Hence, rather than rolling back $\text{Ti}$ as the timestamp ordering protocol would have done, this write operation can be ignored. Otherwise, the protocol is unchanged.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following schedule:
$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{S = (2, W, x),(1, W, z),(1, W, x), C1,(2, W, y),(2, R, y)}
\text{(3, W, z),(3, W, m), C3,(2, R, m), C2}.
\end{gathered}
$$
Where $\text{Ci}$ means commit of $\text{i}^{\text{th}}$ transaction. Triple $\text{(i, W / R, x)}$ means Transaction $\text{i}$ writes/reads item $\text{x}.$
Which of the following statements is/are true for $\text{S}?$

options.text: $\text{S}$ is view serializable but not conflict serializable.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 21)

Check for View serializability :

Transaction $2$ is reading item $m$ which is written by trans $3,$ hence, in the view equivalent serial schedule, Trans $2$ must appear after (not necessarily immediately) Trans $3.\; (3 \rightarrow 2)$

Transaction $1$ is doing the final write of item $x$ which is also written by trans $2,$ hence, in the view equivalent serial schedule, Trans $1$ must appear after(not necessarily immediately) Trans $2. \;(2\rightarrow 1)$

Transaction $3$ is doing the final write of item $z$ which is also written by trans $1,$ hence, in the view equivalent serial schedule, Trans $3$ must appear after(not necessarily immediately) Trans $1. \;(1\rightarrow 3)$

But now we have a contradiction. $3 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 1$ But also $1 \rightarrow 3.$

Hence, Not view serializable.
